name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler
lead: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler is a non-absorbable injectable made of tiny PMMA microspheres suspended in a carrier gel, sold in the United States under names such as Artefill and Bellafill. Because the microspheres are not broken down by the body, the fillers are described as permanent: the particles stay in place and prompt the body to form fibrous tissue around them [3][4][5].

The US FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and for acne scars of the cheek, and it states that removal can be difficult or impossible for permanent fillers [6]. A review of jawline and chin fillers includes PMMA among the materials used in the lower face [2]. PMMA is the same polymer used in bone cement, dentures and other implants, and some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it to shape muscles [5].

Published human evidence on cosmetic PMMA filler in the sources used here is limited to registered studies and reviews. Looksmaxxing forums discuss PMMA mostly as a cautionary subject, for example when a surgeon offered PMMA bone cement for facial implants [8].

paras: PMMA fillers consist of microscopic PMMA beads held in a gel. Rather than being degraded, the particulate scaffold stays in the tissue and provokes fibrous tissue formation around the beads, which supplies the volume [5]. Wikipedia describes the injected microspheres as a soft-tissue filler intended to reduce wrinkles or scars permanently [5].

The FDA states that non-absorbable fillers are approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and that unapproved uses include breast, buttock and foot enhancement and injection into the nose, forehead, periorbital area, neck or muscle [6]. PMMA was also widely used in the early 2000s to restore volume in people with HIV-related facial wasting [5].

A 2023 review of fillers for the chin and jawline covers hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, poly-L-lactic acid and PMMA as options, noting that the advantages of fillers include relatively affordable cost and limited recovery time, and that measures are needed to prevent short- and long-term complications [2].

The FDA's general information on dermal fillers lists bruising, redness, swelling and pain as common; nodules or granulomas, infection and allergic reaction as less common; and filler migration, permanent hard nodules and vascular injury leading to tissue death, vision loss or stroke as rare. It adds that problems can appear weeks, months or years after injection [6]. Because PMMA is not absorbed, any such complication is not self-limiting in the way it can be with temporary fillers, a point the FDA makes about permanent fillers generally [6].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a post-approval study of Artefill for nasolabial folds enrolling 1,008 participants, begun in 2007, with granulomatous disorder as its listed condition [3]. A phase 1 study of Artefill for HIV-associated facial lipoatrophy (31 participants, 2013) is also registered [4]. Results from these registrations are not summarised in the sources used here.

Registered trials of PMMA for gluteal augmentation (one of 137 and one of 133 participants) are listed as not yet recruiting or of unknown status [9][10]; gluteal use is outside the FDA's list of approved filler uses [6]. A 2016 review titled Synthetic Fillers for Facial Rejuvenation covers the category [7].

On looksmax.org, a user reported that his surgeon proposed PMMA bone cement for cheek (infraorbital/malar) implants as a cheaper alternative to PEEK or hydroxyapatite, saying it was biocompatible; the user had heard PMMA was dangerous and asked about side effects, and one reply simply advised against it [8]. That thread concerns bone-cement implants rather than injectable microspheres.

On T Nation, members have said bodybuilder Rich Piana reportedly had PMMA in his arms, and another poster described fear of reduced function from synthol-type injections [11][12]. These are forum statements and are not verified by the sources used here.

lore.intro: PMMA is mentioned in forums mainly in connection with implants and muscle-shaping injections, usually with caution rather than endorsement [8][11][12].

claims.claim: PMMA is dangerous to put in the body
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster said he had heard PMMA was dangerous and asked about side effects when offered it as a facial implant material; a reply said not to use it [8].
claims.experts: The FDA lists granulomas, migration and permanent nodules among the risks of fillers and notes permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible to remove [6]; PMMA is also standard in bone cement and dentures [1][5].

claims.claim: Bodybuilders use PMMA injections to enlarge muscles
claims.believers: T Nation members said Rich Piana was rumoured to have PMMA in his arms [11].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that some bodybuilders illegally use PMMA to shape muscles, and the FDA lists injection into muscle as an unapproved filler use [5][6].

card.summary: Permanent filler beads that stay in the face for good; few sources on outcomes, and removal is difficult if problems arise.
card.note: Permanent: the FDA says removal can be difficult or impossible; granulomas and migration can appear years later.

quick.overview:
PMMA filler is made of tiny plastic beads in a gel. The beads are not absorbed, so the body forms tissue around them and the effect is considered permanent. In the US, permanent fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.

In forums it comes up mostly as a warning: users ask about it when a surgeon offers PMMA bone cement for implants, and bodybuilding forums mention it in connection with muscle-shaping injections.
quick.mechanism: The microspheres act as a scaffold that the body cannot break down; surrounding tissue forms fibrous collagen around them, which adds volume.
quick.risks: The FDA lists lumps, granulomas, infection, migration, permanent hard nodules and rare vascular injury (including blindness) as possible filler complications, some appearing years later. Removal can be difficult or impossible. Use in the buttocks, muscles or other unapproved sites is not sanctioned.
